items.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: he gave me a book called Blues People by Leroi Jones, who is now called Amiri Baraka. And that changed me because the premise of that book is that as African-American people’s lives changed their music changed.

ctx.x: That’s really interesting. I assume you were an aspiring musician before this kind of activism became known to you?

No actually I started piano at the age of 19. And I don’t like to — I’m only providing a context. Because I wasn’t a political activist. It was more like okay here I am in Palo Alto, the white suburbs, and all I see is my block and Leave it to Beaver. This is the reality. Whereas there is all kinds of things that are going around outside my neighborhood. I mean there’s East Palo Alto, an African-American area, and then there’s what’s happening in the world with the Vietnam War and what the United States empire ©…

is doing to other countries. But what was to me a turning point was when my cousin, who is currently an art professor and a friend of mine who is a drummer, introduced to me the music of John Coltrane. And even though I was not politically sophisticated or musically sophisticated at that time, I was only 17 or 18 years old, I was able to see how that music was connected — when I say — see I felt that music was connected with Malcolm X and later on I discovered that Malcolm X and that whole tradition of Harlem…
